extracted.intended_audience: students, critics, and practitioners of art and aesthetics; writers and readers interested in theories of art and beauty
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes competing definitions and evaluative criteria for beauty and art from 18th–19th century aesthetic writers (Kant, Hegel, Schopenhauer, etc.), presenting multiple standards by which artistic value is judged. Useful for theorizing about what counts as art and for critiquing artistic practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three kinds of beauty (Père André)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three kinds of beauty—divine beauty, natural beauty, and artificial beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this tripartite taxonomy when distinguishing sources or types of beauty in works: whether arising from the divine/absolute, from nature itself, or from human-made/artificial composition. No examples beyond naming are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art as imitation of nature (Batteux, Diderot)
rubrics_metrics.description: Art consists in imitating the beauty of nature; its aim being enjoyment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate artworks by how well they imitate or reproduce aspects of nature that generate pleasure. Anti-pattern: judging art solely by non-representational criteria would conflict with this standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste as arbiter of beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty is decided by taste; the laws of taste are not laid down and cannot be settled (view held by many French and English writers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat beauty and merit as contingent on audience/epochal taste. Implication: prescriptive, universal rules are suspect; debates about merit often reflect differing tastes rather than objective criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art unites dispersed beauties (Pagano)
rubrics_metrics.description: Art consists in uniting the beauties dispersed in nature; taste is the capacity to perceive these beauties and artistic genius brings them into one whole; beauty commingles with goodness (beauty as 'goodness made visible').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess artists on their capacity to perceive disparate beauties and synthesize them into a unified whole; moral resonance (goodness) is a relevant dimension of beauty here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art as egotistical sensation (Muratori, Spaletti)
rubrics_metrics.description: Art amounts to an egotistical sensation founded on the desire for self-preservation and society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This psycho-social criterion evaluates art in terms of self-interest and social instinct; useful for readings that emphasize evolutionary/psychological origins of aesthetic response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greatest pleasure = beauty (Hemsterhuis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty is that which gives most pleasure; that which gives most pleasure gives the greatest number of ideas in the shortest time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure aesthetic success by intensity and rapidity of pleasurable idea-generation. Works that stimulate many associations quickly are judged highly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kantian disinterested pleasure / Urteilskraft
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty (subjectively) is that which, necessarily and without reasoning and without practical advantage, pleases; the judging capacity forms judgments without concepts and produces pleasure without desire. Objectively, beauty is the form of an object insofar as it is perceived without any conception of its utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate artworks for 'disinterested' pleasure (pleasure not tied to desire or utility) and for formal qualities perceived independently of usefulness. Anti-pattern: treating beauty as usefulness or practical advantage contradicts Kant here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art as a 'game' whose aim is beauty (Schiller)
rubrics_metrics.description: The aim of art is beauty, the source of which is pleasure without practical advantage; art may be called a game (not trivial but manifestation of life's beauties without other aim).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess art by its ability to manifest beauty as play — purposeless aesthetic pleasure. Works aiming at didactic or utilitarian ends fail this criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty as perception of the infinite in the finite (Schelling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty is the perception of the infinite in the finite; art unites subjective with objective, nature with reason; chief characteristic of works of art is 'unconscious infinity'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value works that suggest or permit apprehension of universals/ideals within particular sensuous forms. Look for implicit transcendence, unity of opposites, and suggestive depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art as manifestation of the beautiful soul and educational aim (Fichte)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty exists not in the world but in the beautiful soul; art is the manifestation of this beautiful soul, and its aim is the education of the whole man (mind, heart, and whole person).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate art on whether it expresses inner moral/spiritual qualities of the artist and contributes to the moral/intellectual education of the audience. Anti-pattern: purely formal virtuosity detached from 'soul' is deficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union of art, nature, and love (Schlegel)
rubrics_metrics.description: The truly beautiful is expressed by the union of art, nature, and love; beauty exists in art, nature, and love together; acknowledges moral and philosophic art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer works that harmonize natural perception, artistic form, and affective (loving) engagement; moral and philosophical content are integral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two kinds of beauty: general and individual (Adam Müller)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are general beauty (universal attraction, e.g., antique art) and individual beauty (resulting from observer becoming a sun attracting beauty — modern art); highest art reproduces universal harmony and is 'art of life'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between works appealing by universal/formal qualities and those relying on individual/subjective resonance; highest praise goes to works that harmonize contradictions into universal coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty as manifestation of the Idea (Hegel and followers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty is the shining of the Idea through matter; only spiritual content is truly beautiful; art is production of the appearance of the Idea; truth and beauty are one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess art for success in embodying abstract Ideas in sensuous forms; works that express philosophical/spiritual truth hold highest status in this scheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty as relations among impressions (Herbart)
rubrics_metrics.description: No beauty existing in itself; beauty arises from certain relations in our impressions—art consists in finding these relations (simultaneous in painting, successive in poetry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate compositional relations (line, colour, sequence) rather than attributing beauty to object-in-itself. Anti-pattern: attributing beauty to mythic associations instead of formal relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty via renunciation and contemplation of Will (Schopenhauer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Renunciation of individuality and contemplation of a plane of manifestation of Will gives perception of beauty; genius can objectivize the Idea on higher planes, producing higher beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value works that enable audience to transcend ego and perceive objectified Will; regard artistic genius as capacity to present higher manifestations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty as artist-produced 'seeming' (Hartmann)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty lies not in the external thing nor in 'the thing in itself' but in the 'seeming' produced by the artist; the artist transforms the thing into beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge art on the artist's transformative power to present objects as beautiful regardless of their external facticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art gives what nature cannot (Schnasse)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no perfect beauty in nature; art discloses beauty by the energy of the free ego conscious of harmony not found in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Esteem works that create harmonious forms beyond natural examples; art's creative, augmentative function is central.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty in music follows unalterable laws (Helmholtz)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty in musical productions is attained only by following unalterable laws; these laws are not known to the artist and beauty is manifested unconsciously, resisting analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For musical evaluation, give weight to adherence to perceptual/physiological laws of harmony and form even if artists cannot articulate them. Recognize limits of conscious compositional analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty perceived subjectively; definition problem (Bergmann)
rubrics_metrics.description: To define beauty objectively is impossible; beauty is perceived subjectively and the aesthetic problem is to define what pleases whom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize empirical and audience-centered approaches to evaluation; be cautious of universal claims about beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty as suprasensible quality producing pleasure (Jungmann)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty is a suprasensible quality of things; it produces pleasure by mere contemplation and is the foundation of love.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value works that elicit contemplative pleasure and ground affective bonds (love); emphasize the contemplative, non-utilitarian response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral foundation and 'variety in unity' (Cousin)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty always has a moral foundation and essentially consists in variety in unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess artworks for moral resonance and formal coherence where diversity of elements is unified into a meaningful whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression of the invisible by natural signs (Jouffroy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty is the expression of the invisible by those natural signs which manifest it; the visible world is the garment by which we see beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the effectiveness of natural signs (lines, colours, motifs) in manifesting invisible truths or qualities; strong metaphorical/expressive economy is prized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art as satisfying love of forms, endowing forms with ideas (Cherbuliez)
rubrics_metrics.description: Art is activity satisfying our innate love of forms, endowing these forms with ideas, and affording pleasure to senses, heart, and reason; beauty is an act of our souls and not absolute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge works across sensory, emotional, and intellectual dimensions; recognize beauty as constructive, subjective act rather than an absolute property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty as innate ideas with unity, variety, and order (Coster)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas of the beautiful, the good, and the true are innate; the idea of Beauty includes unity of essence, variety of constitutive elements, and order bringing unity into various manifestations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use criteria of innate harmony: unity, variety, and order when evaluating artworks; consider metaphysical/teleological dimensions in judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty as physiological/psychological product (Pilo, Grant Allen, Spencer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty is a product of physical feelings or physiological processes; the origin of art is play; aesthetic pleasures have physiological bases; taste can be educated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate psychological and physiological considerations in critique: stimulation, economy of excitation, and habituation. Recognize role of play, excess energy, and educability of taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art as manifestation of emotion via formal media (Véron)
rubrics_metrics.description: Art is the manifestation of emotion transmitted externally by a combination of lines, forms, colours, or by succession of movements, sounds, or words subjected to certain rhythms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how effectively a work externalizes emotion through formal elements and rhythmic organization across media (visual, musical, verbal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of canon-driven definition of art
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing aesthetic standards often reverse the proper method: they accept a canon of favored works and then devise theories to include them, rather than defining art by independent criteria and judging works against them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid retrofitting theories to justify preselected 'great works'; instead define criteria independently (examining causes and effects, aims and purposes) and then judge works. Anti-pattern: using canon membership as sole proof of merit (e.g., excusing immorality because canonical works contain it).

rubrics_metrics.name: Art's aim must be examined via causes and effects, not pleasure alone
rubrics_metrics.description: The aim and importance of art should be understood by examining the activity in itself, its dependence on causes, and connection with effects, rather than defining it by the pleasure it produces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize functional/teleological analysis of art: assess purposes, social/moral effects, and causal relations. Treat pleasure as insufficient basis for judging art's true meaning or value; anti-pattern is equating art's aim with mere gratification.
